 the author is notified through the PR status check, chat or email. Branch protection usually blocks the
 merge until a new push passes, so the fix is to push another commit, which starts the whole pipeline over.
 When everything passes, the pipeline builds one immutable artifact, such as a container image tagged with
 the commit SHA, and stores it in a registry. Every later environment deploys that same artifact.

 The artifact goes to staging first, where smoke tests run against real infrastructure. Production follows,
 either automatically or after a manual approval. The production deploy is often gradual: a canary takes a
 small share of traffic, or a blue-green switch keeps the old version running next to the new one. Health
 checks, error rates and latency are compared against the previous version. If those signals degrade, the
 deploy is rolled back by sending traffic back to the last known-good artifact. This can happen automatically
 when thresholds are crossed, or a person can trigger it. A rollback just redeploys a build that already
 exists, so it takes seconds or minutes. It also doesn't undo database migrations by default, which is why
 teams make schema changes backward-compatible before shipping the code that relies on them.

g.text: stops there and marks the commit red. Nothing after the failed stage runs, no artifact gets promoted, and
the author is notified through the PR status check, chat or email. Branch protection usually blocks the
merge until a new push passes, so the fix is to push another commit, which starts the whole pipeline over.
When everything passes, the pipeline builds one immutable artifact, such as a container image tagged with
the commit SHA, and stores it in a registry. Every later environment deploys that same artifact.
The artifact goes to staging first, where smoke tests run against real infrastructure. Production follows,
either automatically or after a manual approval. The production deploy is often gradual: a canary takes a
small share of traffic, or a blue-green switch keeps the old version running next to the new one. Health
checks, error rates and latency are compared against the previous version. If those signals degrade, the
deploy is rolled back by sending traffic back to the last known-good artifact. This can happen automatically
when thresholds are crossed, or a person can trigger it. A rollback just redeploys a build that already
exists, so it takes seconds or minutes. It also doesn't undo database migrations by default, which is why
teams make schema changes backward-compatible before shipping the code that relies on them.
